```{r setup}
library(geopt)
```

Besides the administrative levels, geopt includes three health geographies.
They're built from the same freguesia boundaries as everything else, so their
borders line up exactly with municipalities and NUTS regions.

* **`uls`**: the 39 Unidades Locais de Saúde (local health units) created by
  the 2024 reform of the national health service (SNS), plus their
  equivalents in the islands, which aren't called ULS: nine Unidades de Saúde
  de Ilha in the Açores ("USI São Miguel", …) and seven centros de saúde in
  Madeira ("CS Funchal Zona I", …). 55 units in total.
* **`reg_saude`**: the 7 health regions (regiões de saúde), with their 2024
  boundaries.
* **`aces`**: the 71 Agrupamentos de Centros de Saúde (groups of primary-care
  centres) that the ULS replaced in 2024. Seven of the 71 are ULS that
  already existed before the reform and took the place of ACES in their area:
  Guarda, Matosinhos, Alto Minho, Nordeste, Baixo Alentejo, Litoral Alentejano
  and Norte Alentejano. ULS de Castelo Branco, which also existed, appears
  through its two ACES.

They work wherever a level is accepted:

```{r uls-map}
plot_pt(level = "uls")
```

## Joining health data

Join by unit name. Names are matched the same way as everywhere else,
ignoring case and accents:

```{r uls-join}
df <- data.frame(uls = c("ULS Coimbra", "uls são joão"), casos = c(340, 120))
m <- get_map("uls", data = df, by = "uls")
plot_pt(m, value = "casos")
```

## Some ULS split municipalities

Lisboa is divided between three ULS: **São José, Santa Maria and Lisboa
Ocidental**. Loures, Porto and Funchal are split too, and so is Gondomar, by a
single freguesia (see below). The `uls` map draws these correctly, because it's
built from freguesias.

This matters when joining data. If it's by municipality, there's no way to
tell which of Lisboa's three ULS a value for Lisboa belongs to. For data by
municipality, use `uls_municipio` instead. It's the same as `uls`, except
that ULS sharing a municipality are combined into one unit:

```{r uls-municipio}
h <- pt_lookup(health_vintage = "2024")
unique(h$unit_municipio[h$unit != h$unit_municipio])
```

ULS Loures-Odivelas is in the first unit, although no part of Lisboa belongs
to it. Combining works in chains: ULS São José also covers four freguesias of
Loures, and the rest of Loures belongs to ULS Loures-Odivelas, so a value for
Loures can't be divided between those two either. Counting the freguesias of
each municipality by ULS shows the chain:

```{r uls-municipio-chain}
u <- unique(h$unit_municipio[h$municipio == "Lisboa"])
lx <- h[h$unit_municipio == u, ]
table(lx$municipio, sub("ULS ", "", lx$unit))
```

Every municipality in the chain gets the combined unit, including those that
lie entirely in one ULS, such as Odivelas and Cascais. Data for Odivelas on
its own would fit ULS Loures-Odivelas, but data for Loures wouldn't, so no
total for ULS Loures-Odivelas can be built from data by municipality.

In `pt_lookup()` these columns are called `unit` and `unit_municipio`,
because with `health_vintage = "2022"` they hold ACES instead of ULS (see
below).

`pt_join()` picks the right column automatically. Joining by freguesia adds `uls`;
joining by municipality adds only `uls_municipio`:

```{r grain}
df <- data.frame(concelho = "Gondomar", v = 1)
out <- pt_join(df, by = c(municipio = "concelho"))
out$uls_municipio
"uls" %in% names(out)
```

To map data by municipality, add up the values by `uls_municipio` and draw
them at `level = "uls_municipio"`, where each combined unit is a single area:

```{r uls-municipio-map}
df <- data.frame(concelho = c("Lisboa", "Odivelas", "Porto", "Maia", "Coimbra"),
                 casos = c(10, 5, 7, 3, 4))
df <- pt_join(df, by = c(municipio = "concelho"))
casos <- aggregate(casos ~ uls_municipio, data = df, FUN = sum)
casos
plot_pt(casos, value = "casos", level = "uls_municipio", by = "uls_municipio")
```

Lisboa and Odivelas add up to one value, for the combined unit, and so do
Porto and Maia.

One freguesia is handled specially. Lomba, in Gondomar, belongs to a
different ULS and ACES from the rest of Gondomar. Taken as it is, it would
combine ULS Vila Nova de Gaia/Espinho with Porto's ULS into one unit, and
ACES Gondomar with ACES Espinho/Gaia. Following established practice,
`uls_municipio` and `aces_municipio` count Lomba with the rest of Gondomar,
which keeps those units separate, and their maps draw it with Gondomar too.
The freguesia-level `uls` and `aces` still place Lomba correctly.

## Before and after the 2024 reform

Before 2024, primary care was organized into ACES, under regional health
administrations (ARS). The 2024 reform replaced them with the ULS, and moved
some municipalities to a different health region. geopt has both versions;
choose one with `health_vintage`:

| `health_vintage` | `unit` holds | `reg_saude` holds | Law |
|---|---|---|---|
| `"2024"` (current) | a ULS, or its island equivalent | the health regions since 2024 | Decreto-Lei 102/2023, which created the ULS |
| `"2022"` | an ACES (71 of them) | the health regions before 2024 | Decreto-Lei 28/2008, which created the ACES |

Four municipalities changed health region in 2024:

```{r vintages}
h24 <- pt_lookup(health_vintage = "2024")
h22 <- pt_lookup(health_vintage = "2022")
d <- data.frame(municipio = h24$municipio,
                reg_saude_2022 = h22$reg_saude[match(h24$dtmnfr, h22$dtmnfr)],
                reg_saude = h24$reg_saude)
d <- d[d$reg_saude != d$reg_saude_2022, ]
unique(d[, c("municipio", "reg_saude_2022", "reg_saude")])
```

ACES names match and join like any other level, so data from before the
reform can go on a map:

```{r aces-join}
df <- data.frame(aces = c("ACES Baixo Vouga", "aces braga"), casos = c(10, 20))
head(pt_join(df, by = "aces"))
```

```{r aces-map, eval = FALSE}
plot_pt(level = "aces")
```

Some ACES also split municipalities, so for data by municipality there's an
`aces_municipio` column, and an `"aces_municipio"` map, that work the same way
as `uls_municipio`:

```{r aces-municipio}
h <- pt_lookup(health_vintage = "2022")
grep(" [+] ", unique(h$unit_municipio), value = TRUE)
```

## Notes and limits

* Every freguesia has both a ULS and an ACES.
* Health regions and ULS don't nest: ULS Médio Tejo is in two health regions
  (Centro and Lisboa e Vale do Tejo). Treat them as separate layers, not as a
  hierarchy.
* The health levels are only available on the current freguesia map, not with
  `get_map(admin_vintage = "2013")`.
